meta.description: No — Shakespeare never wrote this. It’s a garbled paraphrase of Henry van Dyke’s 1901 sundial poem “Time Is.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Time is very slow for those who wait, very fast for those who are scared, very long for those who lament, very short for those who celebrate, but for those who love, time is eternal'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Shakespeare. It’s a reworded version of Henry van Dyke’s sundial poem “Time Is,” first printed 1901.

answer.label: Not William Shakespeare — a garbled Henry van Dyke poem
answer.sourceLine: Shakespeare never wrote this. The lines are a reworded version of Henry van Dyke’s short poem “Time Is,” composed as a sundial inscription and first printed in 1901. Van Dyke’s original reads “too slow … too swift … too long … too short … but for those who love, Time is Eternity”; the Shakespeare-credited version swaps in “scared,” “lament” and “celebrate” and appeared online by 2013. According to Quote Investigator ↗, there is no support for the Shakespeare attribution.

source.excerpt:
Time is
Too Slow for those who Wait,
Too Swift for those who Fear,
Too Long for those who Grieve,
Too Short for those who Rejoice;
But for those who Love,
Time is Eternity.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the lines to Henry van Dyke, first printed in 1901 in Alice Morse Earle’s Old-Time Gardens Newly Set Forth, and finds no support for the Shakespeare attribution.
The poem “Time Is” is published under van Dyke’s name, ending “But for those who Love, / Time is” either “Eternity” or “not” — see the text at American Literature ↗.
On the Folger Shakespeare Library ↗ post on misattributed quotes, a reader flags the “time is eternal” line as “a botched version” of Henry van Dyke.
source.excerptNote: Van Dyke’s original. The widely circulated “Shakespeare” version rewrites “Fear” as “scared,” “Grieve” as “lament,” “Rejoice” as “celebrate,” and “Eternity” as “eternal.” A variant of van Dyke’s own text ends “Time is not.”

source.rightsNote: Van Dyke’s poem “Time Is” was first printed in 1901 and collected in 1904 — both well before 1931 — so the underlying text is in the public domain in the United States. The specific “Shakespeare” wording is simply a later, uncredited corruption of that public-domain poem.

author.name: Henry van Dyke
author.heading: About Henry van Dyke
author.bio: Henry van Dyke was an American Presbyterian clergyman, Princeton professor, and diplomat who served as U.S. Minister to the Netherlands. He wrote widely read devotional and literary works, including the Christmas tale The Other Wise Man and the hymn text “Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee.” His brief sundial meditation on the subjectivity of time became his most quoted lines — and, decades later, a magnet for false attribution to Shakespeare.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s many “Shakespeare” quotes that Shakespeare had nothing to do with. The thought — and nearly all the words — belong to Henry van Dyke.

items.why: The lines appear nowhere in Shakespeare’s plays or poems; the vocabulary (“scared,” “lament,” “celebrate”) is modern. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no evidence for the Shakespeare credit, which spread online by 2013.

Van Dyke wrote “too slow … too swift … too long … too short … but for those who love, Time is Eternity.” The circulating version replaces “fear/grieve/rejoice” with “scared/lament/celebrate” and “Eternity” with “eternal” — a garble, not a quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Henry van Dyke, whose sundial poem “Time Is” was in print by 1901 ↗ — not William Shakespeare.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Van Dyke’s lines were composed for a sundial — an object whose whole purpose is to mark time — and they turn that function into a meditation on how differently time feels depending on our state of mind. The final turn, that for lovers time becomes eternity, is what made the poem endure.

The verse gained fresh fame when it was read at the 1997 funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, which helped push it into wide circulation — and, as often happens with a beloved line, some reposters eventually pinned it on Shakespeare.
